newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt awards contracts for Asia-Africa bridge.
newsitem.headline: Egypt awards contracts for Asia-Africa bridge.

text.p: Egypt has contracted two local firms to build part of a $150 million suspension bridge to link Africa with Asia and is waiting for Japan to offer finance before the project can go ahead, officials said on Wednesday.

The 3.90 km (2.4 miles) bridge, set 70 metres (230 feet) above the waters of the Suez Canal so that the largest ships can pass, will be the first overland road link between Africa and Asia since the canal was built in the 1860s.
The only links between African Egypt and the Sinai peninsula are now the Ahmed Hamdi tunnel and ferries.

Fouad Abdel Aziz Khalil, chairman of the government's General Authority for Roads and Bridges, told Reuters the state last week awarded state-owned Arab Contractors-Osman Ahmed Osman the contract to build the eastern approach bridge. General Nile Roads and Bridges will build the western approach.

Official documents on the project have said the local firms will build the approaches up to a height of 49.5 metres (162 feet). A Japanese contractor will build the rest of the approach bridges and the main middle section of the bridge.
Egyptian and Japanese officials have contradicated each other on the Japanese involvement in the project finance but Japanese diplomatic sources said the grant was close to being officially approved.
"Both countries have yet to exchange official notes -- a bureaucratic procedure. The grant will almost certainly be given to Egypt," one diplomat said.
Egypt says that Japan would pay for a large part of the project through an aid grant which Tokyo says it has not yet decided on.
The source declined to say how much it would be but Khalil said it would foot the bill for the main middle section of the bridge and other costs.

"Only Japanese firms are eligible to tender for the rest of the bridge because of the grant which will cover about more than half the costs...they (Japanese government) will open the tender for the bridge soon, probably in July," Khalil added.
The bridge, with four lanes, will be near the town of Qantara, 47 km (29 miles) south of Port Said city.

It will serve mainly northern Sinai, where the government is planning to irrigate 400,000 acres (160,000 hectares). The population of all Sinai is expected to rise to 3.2 million in 2017 from a few hundred thousand today.
The documents say traffic across the canal is expected to reach 50,000 vehicles a day in 2015. The ferries can take 12,000 and the tunnel about 10,000, leaving 28,000 for the bridge.
They say it will take 42 months to build the bridge, including six months for preparations.
